topic: What if you fell into a black hole?
title: WHAT IF YOU
FELL INTO A BLACK HOLE?

script.text: You're falling toward a black hole. Don't panic. Here's exactly what happens.
What if you fell into a black hole?
First, the stars bend. Light curves around the hole, and the sky stretches into rings.
Then you cross the event horizon. No wall. No bump. You just can't come back. Even light can't escape from here.
Your best friend watches from far away. You slow down. You turn red. You fade. They never see you cross.
Inside, it gets worse. Gravity pulls your feet far harder than your head. You stretch like spaghetti.
Around a small black hole, that difference is over twenty million times Earth's gravity. That's real.
But fall into a giant one, like the monster at the centre of our galaxy, and you'd feel almost nothing.
From the edge, you'd have at most sixty-six seconds. Then the centre, where our physics breaks down.
Nobody knows what happens next. Want to find out?

science.claim: Light bends around a black hole (gravitational lensing), so background stars are smeared into arcs and rings.
science.working: General relativity: mass curves spacetime and light follows the curved paths. Observed routinely as gravitational lensing; the Event Horizon Telescope images of M87* and Sgr A* show the lensed ring of light.

science.claim: At the event horizon the escape speed equals the speed of light, so nothing, not even light, can leave.
science.working: Definition of the Schwarzschild radius r_s = 2GM/c^2: escape speed sqrt(2GM/r) = c at r = r_s. Nothing local marks the crossing for a freely falling observer: no wall, no bump.
science.source: Schwarzschild (1916); standard GR textbooks (e.g. Hartle, Gravity)

science.claim: A distant friend sees you slow down, redden and fade, and never sees you cross.
science.working: Gravitational time dilation and redshift diverge at the horizon for a far observer: signals from an infalling object are stretched to infinite wavelength and delay, so the object appears to freeze and fade just outside r_s.
science.source: standard GR result for the Schwarzschild metric; e.g. Hamilton & Lisle (2008), The river model of black holes

science.claim: Around a small black hole, the tidal difference across your body at the horizon is over twenty million times Earth's gravity.
science.working: Tidal acceleration across length L at radius r: a = 2GM L / r^3. For M = 10 solar masses, r = r_s = 2GM/c^2 = 29.5 km, L = 2 m: a = 2.06e8 m/s^2 = 2.1e7 g (21 million g). Run: G = 6.674e-11, c = 2.998e8, Msun = 1.989e30 kg. Per the script: 'a small black hole' = about ten solar masses; 'over twenty million' holds (21 million).
science.source: Newtonian tidal approximation, accurate in order of magnitude at the horizon of a Schwarzschild hole; cross-check: Astronomy magazine, 'Why are small black holes more dangerous than big ones?' (Feb 2023)

science.claim: Falling into a supermassive black hole like Sagittarius A*, you would feel almost nothing at the horizon.
science.working: Sgr A* mass 4.297 million solar masses (GRAVITY Collaboration). r_s = 1.27e10 m (12.7 million km). Tidal acceleration across 2 m at the horizon = 2GM L / r^3 = 1.1e-3 m/s^2 = about 0.0001 g, far less than the pull you feel on Earth. (Tidal force at the horizon scales as 1/M^2.)
science.source: GRAVITY Collaboration (2021, 2023), Sgr A* mass 4.297 million Msun; own calculation

science.claim: From the horizon to the centre takes at most about sixty-six seconds for Sgr A*.
science.working: Maximum proper time from the horizon to the singularity for radial infall is tau = pi G M / c^3. For M = 4.297e6 Msun: pi x 4.925e-6 s x 4.297e6 = 66.5 s. Falling in from rest at the horizon gives the maximum; other paths give less, hence 'at most'.
science.source: Schwarzschild geodesics (cycloid solution); Lewis & Kwan (2007), 'No way back: maximizing survival time below the Schwarzschild event horizon', arXiv:0705.1029

science.claim: At the centre our physics breaks down: nobody knows what happens.
science.working: GR predicts a curvature singularity; a quantum theory of gravity would be needed to describe it and does not yet exist.
science.source: standard statement of the open problem; e.g. Hawking & Ellis (1973), The Large Scale Structure of Space-Time
